surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (Latin America)
surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A business-to-consumer (B2C) market research questionnaire about Running Shoes. Every question asks about Running Shoes specifically — not the wider market, not adjacent categories, and not any named brand. It is designed to tell a client what buyers in Latin America actually do and want in this category.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Latin America who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults who have bought running shoes for themselves in the past 12 months; Adults who run or jog regularly (at least once a week) and intend to buy running shoes in the next 6 months; Adults who consider running shoes as their primary athletic footwear for exercise. Excluded: Children under 18 (unless buying for themselves, but typically parent proxy); Professional athletes or elite runners (niche, not representative of mass market); Institutional buyers (e.g., gyms, schools, military) – not consumer segment; People who only buy running shoes for fashion without any running activity.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Running shoes are purchased by individual consumers for personal athletic and casual use. While some running shoes are sold to institutions (e.g., for team sports), the dominant market is everyday consumers buying for themselves.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least once a week
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness or casual wear
Researches product reviews and compares brands before buying
Values performance features (cushioning, support, weight) and brand reputation
May participate in running events or use fitness apps
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income — these define who was recruited, not what is measured, so they appear in the audience definition rather than as questions.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running and how it fits into their life, then moves into their shoe usage context. It then traces the purchase journey from trigger through discovery, research, channel, and decision, ending with spend and loyalty. Next, it explores what they demand from a shoe—features, fit, quality, style, claims—and how they trade off and value these. Finally, it assesses their satisfaction, pain points, and future intentions, closing with advocacy and forward-looking behavior.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in Latin America — who Adults who have bought running shoes for themselves in the past 12 months; Adults who run or jog regularly (at least once a week) and intend to buy running shoes in the next 6 months; Adults who consider running shoes as their primary athletic footwear for exercise. The consumer market for running shoes is broad, spanning casual joggers to serious amateurs. The audience is defined by personal use and purchase, with a focus on regular runners who are likely to have recent purchase intent. Excluding professional athletes keeps the survey representative of the mass consumer market.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how running fits into your life right now?
options: I run occasionally, mostly for fun or to stay active
I run a few times a month to keep in shape
I run at least once a week as part of my routine
I run several times a week and take it seriously
I train for races or competitions regularly
I don't run currently, but I'm thinking about starting

data.label: I run occasionally, mostly for fun or to stay active
I run a few times a month to keep in shape
I run at least once a week as part of my routine
I run several times a week and take it seriously
I train for races or competitions regularly
I don't run currently, but I'm thinking about starting

questions.insight: Top response: I run occasionally, mostly for fun or to stay active (28.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Casual and health-oriented personas (Budget-Conscious Beginner, Family-Focused, Health-Motivated) dominate occasional/few-times-a-month; Aspiring Amateur and Urban Professional drive serious/race segments.

questions.question: In a typical week, on how many days do you wear running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: 3-4 days (32.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Most wear running shoes a few days a week for casual/errands; daily wear driven by style-driven and health-motivated personas.

questions.question: In a typical week, which of the following activities do you use your running shoes for? Select all that apply.
options: Running on a treadmill or indoor track
Going to the gym or doing other workouts
Wearing them casually (work, school, social outings)

data.label: Running on a treadmill or indoor track
Going to the gym or doing other workouts
Wearing them casually (work, school, social outings)

questions.insight: Top response: Walking (for exercise or errands) (65.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Select-all rates reflect multi-use: walking and casual wear are high across family/casual personas; running-specific uses driven by serious runners.

questions.question: Who in your household runs or jogs regularly (at least once a month)? Select all that apply.
options: No one in my household runs or jogs

data.label: No one in my household runs or jogs

questions.insight: Top response: I do (60.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Self is primary runner; family-focused personas increase partner/children rates; some households have no runners.

questions.question: When choosing running shoes for yourself or someone in your household, who usually has the most influence on the final decision?
options: No one – we rarely buy running shoes

data.label: No one – we rarely buy running shoes

questions.insight: Top response: I do (70.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Self-decision dominates; family influence modest; local store loyalists may rely on salesperson but small weight.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes your main reason for running?
options: To improve my fitness and stay in shape
To relieve stress and clear my head
To train for races or competitions
To spend time with friends or a running group
To enjoy being outdoors and exploring

data.label: To improve my fitness and stay in shape
To relieve stress and clear my head
To train for races or competitions
To spend time with friends or a running group
To enjoy being outdoors and exploring

questions.insight: Top response: To improve my fitness and stay in shape (45.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Fitness is primary across health and family personas; stress relief and outdoors appeal to casual/eco personas; race training small.

questions.question: Which of the following most often prompts you to buy a new pair of running shoes?
options: My current pair is worn out or no longer comfortable
I have a new running goal or training plan
I just want a new pair for style or motivation
I found a good deal or discount

data.label: My current pair is worn out or no longer comfortable
I have a new running goal or training plan
I just want a new pair for style or motivation
I found a good deal or discount

questions.insight: Top response: My current pair is worn out or no longer comfortable (42.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Worn-out/comfort triggers dominate across budget, family, and health personas; deal-seeking is boosted by value and budget personas.

questions.question: Before you decide to buy a new pair of running shoes, where do you typically first hear about or see new options? Select the one that applies most often.
options: Online ads or social media posts
In a physical store (seeing them on display)
Running or fitness websites and blogs

data.label: Online ads or social media posts
In a physical store (seeing them on display)
Running or fitness websites and blogs

questions.insight: Top response: Online ads or social media posts (30.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Online ads and social media are strong for mainstream and early adopters; local store loyalists and family-focused rely on in-store and word-of-mouth.

questions.question: How much time do you typically spend researching and comparing running shoes (reading reviews, checking fit guides, comparing prices) before you buy a new pair?
options: I don't research — I buy what looks or feels right at the store
More than 3 hours, spread over several days

data.label: I don't research — I buy what looks or feels right at the store
More than 3 hours, spread over several days

questions.insight: Top response: 30 minutes to 1 hour (25.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Moderate research time is common; online research savvy and aspiring athletes spend more time, while local store loyalists and budget buyers decide quickly.

questions.question: Where do you actually buy your running shoes most often?
options: Online — from a dedicated running or sports retailer
Online — from a general marketplace or department store website
In a general sports or department store
In a local market or independent shoe shop

data.label: Online — from a dedicated running or sports retailer
Online — from a general marketplace or department store website
In a general sports or department store
In a local market or independent shoe shop

questions.insight: Top response: In a general sports or department store (25.00%).
questions.distributionNote: General sports/department stores and online marketplaces are popular for price-sensitive and mainstream personas; local stores retain loyalists and older segments.

questions.question: How often do you typically buy a new pair of running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: About once a year (32.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Annual or every-1-2-year cycles are typical; budget and family personas stretch intervals, while enthusiasts and professionals replace more often.

questions.question: When you are choosing a new pair of running shoes, which ONE factor most often decides which shoe you pick?
options: Durability and how long it will last

data.label: Durability and how long it will last

questions.insight: Top response: Comfort and cushioning (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Comfort is the top driver across most personas; price is strong for budget and family segments, while performance matters to athletes and professionals.

questions.question: Roughly how much do you typically spend on a new pair of running shoes?
questions.insight: Top response: $60 to $99 (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Price sensitivity pushes most toward $30-$99; upper-middle personas and enthusiasts are willing to spend $100+.

questions.question: When you buy a new pair of running shoes, how often do you stick with the same model you bought before?
questions.insight: Top response: Sometimes the same, sometimes different (30.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Brand-loyal personas (local store loyalists, aspiring athletes) stick with models; style-driven and online researchers are more likely to switch.

questions.question: Which of the following features are non-negotiable for you in a running shoe? Select all that apply.
questions.insight: Top response: Cushioning that absorbs impact (78.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Comfort and fit dominate across personas; hot climate runner and budget-conscious drive breathability; wide foot seeker and health-motivated drive arch support.

questions.question: When choosing a running shoe, how important is cushioning to you?
questions.insight: Top response: Very important (45.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Family-focused, health-motivated, and budget-conscious prioritize cushioning; performance-oriented also value it, but some style-driven and eco-conscious are less focused.

questions.question: When you are judging how well a running shoe fits, which of the following matters most to you?
options: The length is true to size
The width fits my foot comfortably
The heel stays snug without slipping
The toe box gives my toes enough room
The arch support lines up with my foot

data.label: The length is true to size
The width fits my foot comfortably
The heel stays snug without slipping
The toe box gives my toes enough room
The arch support lines up with my foot

questions.insight: Top response: The width fits my foot comfortably (30.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Wide foot seeker and value-seeking family drive width importance; length and toe box also matter for comfort-focused personas; arch support less prioritized.

questions.question: When you think about the materials and construction of a running shoe, which of the following would make you doubt how long it will last? Select all that apply.
options: Thin or flimsy sole that bends too easily
Visible glue marks or loose stitching
Mesh that feels fragile or see-through
Sole that feels hard and brittle

data.label: Thin or flimsy sole that bends too easily
Visible glue marks or loose stitching
Mesh that feels fragile or see-through
Sole that feels hard and brittle

questions.insight: Top response: Thin or flimsy sole that bends too easily (70.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Durability concerns are high across budget-conscious and family personas; flimsy sole and poor construction are top red flags; hot climate runner also worries about fragile mesh.

questions.question: How important is the look and color of a running shoe to you, especially when wearing them beyond running?
questions.insight: Top response: Moderately important (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Style-driven casual and urban professional push importance; but budget and performance personas care less, resulting in a moderate peak.

questions.question: Which of the following claims or certifications would make you more likely to choose one running shoe over another? Select all that apply.
options: Designed for durability and long life
None of these would influence my choice

data.label: Designed for durability and long life
None of these would influence my choice

questions.insight: Top response: Designed for durability and long life (60.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Durability claim resonates with budget and family personas; ethical and recycled claims appeal to eco-conscious and urban professionals; many remain skeptical.

questions.question: If you had to choose between two running shoes that both fit well, which trade-off would you be most willing to make?
options: Pay more for a shoe that lasts longer
Give up some cushioning for a lighter shoe
Choose a less stylish shoe to get better performance
Choose a more sustainable shoe even if it costs more
Choose a cheaper shoe even if it wears out sooner

data.label: Pay more for a shoe that lasts longer
Give up some cushioning for a lighter shoe
Choose a less stylish shoe to get better performance
Choose a more sustainable shoe even if it costs more
Choose a cheaper shoe even if it wears out sooner

questions.insight: Top response: Pay more for a shoe that lasts longer (40.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Durability is top priority for budget and family personas; performance-oriented choose performance over style; some price-sensitive choose cheaper option.

questions.question: Considering a running shoe that meets all your functional needs, which price range would you consider a fair price to pay?
questions.insight: Top response: $50 to $79 (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: High price sensitivity and middle income push majority to under $110; upper-middle personas allow higher but still value-conscious.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied are you with the running shoes you currently use?
questions.insight: Top response: Somewhat dissatisfied (28.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Price-sensitive and durability-focused personas (Budget-Conscious Beginner 14%, Family-Focused 10%, Value-Seeking 10%) skew toward dissatisfaction; comfort-driven and brand-loyal personas (Local Store Loyalist 9%, Aspiring Amateur 8%) add moderate satisfaction.

The sizing is inconsistent or hard to get right
They wear out or lose cushioning too quickly

options: A noticeably better fit or more size options

questions.question: How likely are you to recommend your current running shoes to a friend or family member who is looking for a new pair?
questions.insight: Top response: Somewhat unlikely (25.00%).

questions.question: In the next 12 months, how likely are you to increase how often you run?
questions.insight: Top response: Somewhat likely (35.00%).

options: I will run more often and need more running shoes

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running and how it fits into their life, then moves into their shoe usage context. It then traces the purchase journey from trigger through discovery, research, channel, and decision, ending with spend and loyalty. Next, it explores what they demand from a shoe—features, fit, quality, style, claims—and how they trade off and value these. Finally, it assesses their satisfaction, pain points, and future intentions, closing with advocacy and forward-looking behavior.
storyline_notes: Added a category-specific 'fit_and_sizing' beat in preferences_expectations because fit and sizing are top pain points in the region and critical for footwear.

In consumer_profile, split 'usage_occasion' into two beats: 'running_occasions' (when/why they run) and 'shoe_usage_context' (whether shoes are used only for running or also casual), to capture the dual-use reality in Latin America.
In buying_behavior, added a separate 'research_process' beat to reflect the high research effort and online review usage among the target audience, while keeping 'discovery_channels' distinct.
Moved 'spend_band' later in buying_behavior, after decision drivers, to respect sensitivity around money.
In preferences_expectations, added 'style_and_aesthetics' as a distinct beat because many consumers wear running shoes casually, and style is a top purchase driver.
In satisfaction_future_intent, kept the canonical order but ensured 'switching_triggers' comes before 'recommend_intent' to avoid priming advocacy with switching thoughts.
metadata.classification_reason: Running shoes are purchased by individual consumers for personal athletic and casual use. While some running shoes are sold to institutions (e.g., for team sports), the dominant market is everyday consumers buying for themselves.
